newsitem.title: USA: Hughes rises amid speculation on bid war.
newsitem.headline: Hughes rises amid speculation on bid war.

text.p: Hughes Electronics Corp's share price rose two points to 63 Thursday on speculation that Northrop Grumman Corp and Raytheon Co had begun a bidding war over Hughes's missile and defense-electronics operations.
The Wall Street Journal said Raytheon had bid $9 billion and that Northrop Grumman had offered as much as $9.5 billion.
Hughes's corporate parent, General Motors Corp, and Raytheon declined comment on the report.
"I don't think it's necessarily the high bidder that will win," said Paul Nisbet, a defense analyst at JSA Research.
Analysts say Raytheon may have an edge because of its comparative financial strength and GM's desire to avoid a hefty tax bill.

They say that in order to avoid paying about $2 billion of capital gains taxes that would result from a cash sale of Hughes, GM wants to load up the unit with as much as $5 billion in debt. Hughes has just $200 million of debt at present.
The acquiring company would issue stock to make up the balance of the purchase price, analysts said.

"For Northrop to issue $4-$6 billion (in stock), they would actually have to issue enough stock to give a majority holding to General Motors. Whereas Raytheon would have to give about 30 percent of their holdings (to GM)," Nisbet said.
It is unlikely that GM would want to hold a majority interest in Northrop, he said.
"It would seem to me that Raytheon can come in lower than Northrop and still get it," he said.
Northrop has about $3.3 billion in debt and $1.6 billion in shareholder equity.

Raytheon, even after this week's agreement to buy Texas Instruments Inc's defense assets for $2.95 billion, has about $6.5 billion of debt and $4.6 billion in shareholder equity, making it comparatiely less loaded with debt than Northrop.

Raytheon is also seen to have another advantage -- it could sell off a non-defense business such as its Engineers & Contructors unit for over $3 billion, softening the heavy debt load that would come with buying Hughes.
"I think Raytheon has the uppper hand just because of that," said William Fiala, an analyst at brokerage firm Edward Jones. "Their options are almost limitless."
In midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange, Raytheon shares were down 1-3/4 at 47, Northrop was off 1-1/4 at 78.
